name: Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Act 45 of 1860) — full text as in force to 2024-06-30
publisher: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India
time_latest: 2024-06-30 (repealed by BNS s.358 with effect from 2024-07-01)
license: unstated (Government of India enactment; enactments are freely reproducible)
caveats: Repealed 2024-07-01, but BNSS s.531 savings mean IPC FIRs keep being registered and investigated for years — IPC section numbers appear in CII 2024, 2025 and beyond
23 chapters / 511 sections; four chapters (VIII, XIV, XVI, XVII) plus XX-A and XXII carry ~95% of what a crime map shows

Snatching has no IPC section — it was booked as theft (379) or robbery (392) or under state amendments (Delhi 356/379A/379B, Punjab/Haryana 379A/379B, Maharashtra), so any pre-2024 snatching series is state-law-dependent and not nationally comparable
State amendments mean 'the IPC' is not textually identical across states
evidence: Not fetched. indiacode.nic.in / Legislative Department / MHA are egress-blocked in the session that wrote the dossier. Act number, structure and the section lists in dossier section 1.1 are recorded from model knowledge plus the Wikipedia BNS article that was read.
how_to_obtain: Fetch the consolidated text from indiacode.nic.in (search 'Indian Penal Code 1860') or the Legislative Department site from a network without the session egress proxy. For the state-amended variants, each state's law department publishes its own amendment acts; the Delhi/Punjab/Haryana snatching amendments must be collected individually.
notes: We need the section-level text only to build statute_xwalk (dossier section 7.3) and to label crime heads; we do not need a full statutory database.

name: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Act 45 of 2023)
publisher: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India
license: unstated (Government of India enactment; enactments are freely reproducible)
caveats: Contains NO schedule of correspondences to the IPC — s.358 simply repeals it. There is no statutory IPC->BNS concordance
358 sections in 20 chapters; offences against women and children pulled into a single chapter V (ss.63-99) that the IPC scattered across chapters XVI, XVII and XX-A

Creates offences with no IPC predecessor: 304 snatching, 111 organised crime, 112 petty organised crime, 113 terrorist act, 69 sex by deceitful means, 103(2) mob lynching — any 2024->2025 growth chart for these is an artefact of the statute book

BNS 106(2) (hit-and-run causing death) was held in abeyance after the January 2024 transporters' strike and was NOT brought into force with the rest of the Sanhita; confirm status before ingesting any 106 data
The Wikipedia rendering of the arrangement of sections is offset by one chapter and must be checked against the gazette before shipping
evidence: Not fetched directly; indiacode.nic.in, MHA and the Legislative Department are egress-blocked. Act number (45 of 2023), 1 July 2024 commencement, 358 sections / 20 chapters and two concordance rows (BNS 63 <- IPC 375, BNS 147 <- IPC 121) come from the English Wikipedia 'Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita' article, which was read on 2026-09-19.
how_to_obtain: Download the gazette text from indiacode.nic.in or egazette.gov.in from an unproxied network. The chapter/section arrangement must be taken from the gazette, not from Wikipedia (the Wikipedia arrangement is off by one chapter).
notes: The single most important statute artefact in the project: every post-2024-07-01 crime row is keyed on BNS sections.

name: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Act 46 of 2023)
publisher: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India
license: unstated (Government of India enactment; enactments are freely reproducible)
caveats: s.531 savings clause keeps the IPC/CrPC alive for offences committed before 2024-07-01 — CII 2024 and CII 2025 are genuinely mixed-statute datasets

s.173 replaces CrPC s.154 (mandatory FIR registration); s.173(3) re-introduces a discretionary preliminary inquiry of up to 14 days for cognizable offences punishable with 3-7 years — a partial statutory rollback of Lalita Kumari that may DEPRESS registered crime from 2024-07-01 onward
s.173 also underpins the Zero FIR, which our crime_event schema flags (is_zero_fir)
531 sections, 39 chapters, 2 schedules
evidence: Not fetched; sources egress-blocked. Act number, size and the s.173(3)/s.531 provisions are recorded in dossier sections 1.2 and 6.2 from model knowledge.
how_to_obtain: Download from indiacode.nic.in or egazette.gov.in from an unproxied network. s.173 and s.531 are the only two sections the pipeline actually needs to quote.
notes: Matters to us as a *statistical* artefact, not a procedural one: s.173(3) is a candidate explanation for any fall in registered crime in 2024-25, and must be carried as the series_break_flag 'bnss_prelim_inquiry_2024'.

publisher: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India
geo_coverage: Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh (with all-India consequences for the state/UT panel)

name: Sankalan — compendium / bridge between the old and new criminal laws (app + PDF)
publisher: National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Ministry of Home Affairs
caveats: NOT VERIFIED. The dossier could not confirm this artefact exists in the form described: ncrb.gov.in is egress-blocked
Even if it exists, it is a compendium published by a statistics bureau, not a statutory schedule — it has no legal force and may differ from how any given SHO charged a case
If it turns out to be app-only, the mapping may have to be extracted from the app bundle rather than a document
evidence: Not fetched: ncrb.gov.in is blocked by the dossier session's egress proxy. The dossier records from model knowledge that NCRB/MHA released a compendium named 'Sankalan' as an app plus PDF around the 1 July 2024 rollout, billed as a bridge between the old and new laws, and explicitly flags verifying it as Phase-2 task #1.
how_to_obtain: Phase-2 task #1. (a) Browse ncrb.gov.in from an Indian/unproxied network and look for the new-criminal-laws or publications section; (b) check the Google Play / App Store listing for an NCRB 'Sankalan' app and extract its section tables; (c) failing both, file an RTI with NCRB (CPIO, NCRB, NH-8 Mahipalpur, New Delhi) asking for the IPC-to-BNS correspondence table used in CII 2024 compilation. (c) is the request that actually matters, because it asks for the table NCRB itself used.
notes: THE key open question of this domain: there is no statutory IPC->BNS concordance, so whatever NCRB used to compile CII 2024 is the nearest thing to an official mapping in existence.

name: IPC -> BNS concordance table (hand-built, ~110 rows, dossier section 1.3)
publisher: India Crime Map project (this repository)
caveats: Assembled by hand from model knowledge of both statutes. Only TWO rows are independently web-verified (BNS 63 <- IPC 375, BNS 147 <- IPC 121, both from Wikipedia). MHA, India Code, Legislative Department, NCRB and UP Police were all egress-blocked
Rows carry a confidence column H/M/L; do not ship the table without checking it against NCRB Sankalan or the gazette

The relation is many-to-many, not a function: IPC 383-389 -> BNS 308; IPC 453-460 -> BNS 331; IPC 364/364A/365/367 -> BNS 140. Post-2024 property-crime data is permanently lower-resolution than pre-2024 data

Relation codes: = exact, subset, superset, M many->one (resolution lost), S one->several, NEW (no IPC predecessor), GONE (no BNS successor). IPC 377 and 497 are GONE; IPC 124A has only a differently-worded successor (BNS 152) — those series die at 2024-06-30
The only robust unit of comparison across the 2024 boundary is our own L2 group, never the section and never the L3 head
evidence: Read in full at /home/user/Crime-map/research/sources/taxonomy-methodology.md section 1.3 on 2026-09-19: five sub-tables (homicide and hurt; kidnapping/abduction/trafficking; sexual offences; property; public order/state/intimidation/documents) with IPC, offence, BNS, relation, confidence and note columns.
how_to_obtain: Already held: research/sources/taxonomy-methodology.md section 1.3. Load it into statute_xwalk(from_statute, from_section, to_statute, to_section, relation, comparable, source, confidence) as described in dossier section 7.3.
notes: Today this is the ONLY IPC->BNS mapping the project actually possesses. Treat it as a draft to be replaced, row by row, by Sankalan / the gazette / state-police tables.

name: Crime in India — 'Concepts and Definitions' / explanatory note (principal offence rule, denominators, city panel)
publisher: National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Ministry of Home Affairs
caveats: States the principal offence rule: the counting unit is the FIR (case), not the offence, and only the most severely punishable offence in an FIR is counted, once. Every subordinate offence in that FIR becomes statistically invisible
NCRB publishes NO estimate of how much the rule undercounts, and the dossier found no official one
States (with high but unconfirmed confidence) the denominators NCRB uses: projected mid-year population for India and States/UTs, but CENSUS 2011 population for districts and for metropolitan cities

The metropolitan-city panel definition changed at CII 2014 from 53 'mega cities' (1M+, Census 2011) to 19 'metropolitan cities' (2M+, Census 2011); the exact list and threshold still need checking against the volume
Wording changes between editions — quote the edition, not 'NCRB says'
evidence: Not fetched: ncrb.gov.in is blocked by the dossier session's egress proxy. Dossier sections 2.1, 3.3 and 5.1 record the content from model knowledge and flag each claim for confirmation against the volume.
how_to_obtain: Download any Crime in India volume PDF from ncrb.gov.in (or the data.gov.in mirror) from an unproxied network and read the front matter. Do this for at least CII 2013, 2016, 2022 and 2024 — the explanatory note is where definition changes are announced, so diffing editions is how we find breaks we do not yet know about.
notes: This short piece of front matter is the legal-methodological basis for every caveat the product displays. It is a higher priority than any single data table.

name: NCRB crime-head labels (Group_Name / Sub_Group_Name strings in Crime in India table extracts)
publisher: National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Ministry of Home Affairs
caveats: NCRB does NOT publish a stable numeric crime-head code dictionary. In the report heads are identified by a serial number within a table; in machine-readable extracts by label strings that drift between editions ('Rape' -> 'Rape (Sec 376 IPC)' -> 'Rape (Sec.376 IPC)')

The practical primary key is a (year, raw_label) pair and it is unstable — we must build and maintain ncrb_head_alias(year, raw_label, source_table_ref, crime_key) ourselves, and an unmapped label must FAIL THE BUILD

Three nesting levels behave differently: sub-head -> head sums, head -> chapter total sums, ACROSS chapters does not (cross-cut chapters such as Crime against Women, Children, SC/ST, Cyber, Economic, Human Trafficking are views over the same FIRs; adding them to Total IPC Crimes produces a number that exists nowhere)
Aggregation is only permitted within a single source_table_ref; every fact row must carry source_table_ref and rollup_safe
evidence: Nothing fetched: ncrb.gov.in is egress-blocked. Dossier section 1.5 asserts from model knowledge both that no stable code dictionary is published and how the labels drift, giving the 'Rape (Sec 376 IPC)' example.
how_to_obtain: There is no dictionary to download — it has to be reconstructed. Harvest the distinct Group_Name/Sub_Group_Name values from every Crime in India table extract we ingest (see the ncrb-national dossier for the volumes and mirrors), one label set per (year, table), and hand-map each to our crime_key. Budget this as a real piece of work: it is the single largest hand-mapping task in the project.
notes: Companion artefact to the statute concordance: sections map to crime_key through statute_xwalk, NCRB labels map to crime_key through ncrb_head_alias, and neither mapping may be inferred at runtime.

name: Population Projections for India and States 2011-2036 — Report of the Technical Group on Population Projections
publisher: National Commission on Population, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India
caveats: DOES NOT GO BELOW STATE LEVEL. There are no official district population projections in India at all — this is the central denominator problem
Projections by state/UT, sex, five-year age group, with a rural/urban split, to 2036
Built on a Census 2011 base and pre-COVID assumptions; the 2021 census never happened, so nothing has re-based it
This is the projection NCRB itself uses for India and State/UT rates — but NOT for district or metropolitan-city rates, where it uses raw Census 2011
Reference population figures quoted in the dossier mix TG output with UN WPP 2024 estimates; each must be checked against the TG report before use
evidence: Not fetched. The dossier names the report precisely (title, Technical Group, National Commission on Population / MoHFW, July 2020) and its contents; the population reference points around it are attributed to the Wikipedia 'Demographics of India' article read on 2026-09-19.
how_to_obtain: Search main.mohfw.gov.in / nhm.gov.in / the National Commission on Population pages for 'Population Projections for India and States 2011-2036'; it is a public PDF and is widely mirrored (NITI Aayog, MoSPI). Extract the state x year x rural/urban tables to CSV — they are the growth factors in step 2 of the denominator recipe in dossier section 3.5.
notes: Step 2 of the project's denominator method. Not covered by any other dossier in this repository.

name: Census of India 2011 — Primary Census Abstract (PCA), district and village/town tables
publisher: Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India (ORGI), Ministry of Home Affairs
caveats: 15.5 years old as of 2026-09-19 and it is still the ONLY real district-level population count India has; there will be no replacement before ~2028
Uses the 640-district 2011 geometry — 160 districts (+25%) have been created since, so one district in five on a current map has no 2011 population of its own

Using it raw as a 2025/26 denominator inflates every rate by ~19-21% uniformly (harmless, a labelling error) AND by a further 40-80% differentially in fast-growing peri-urban districts (Gurugram, Gautam Buddha Nagar, Bengaluru Urban, Rangareddy, Medchal-Malkajgiri, Thane, Surat, Ghaziabad, Pune) relative to slow-growing ones. That differential is a defamation-grade error
NCRB's published district and metropolitan-city rates use exactly this raw 2011 denominator — which is why the dossier's recommendation is to compute our own rates and not use NCRB's
The city denominator is a Census urban agglomeration, a different polygon from the police commissionerate that produces the numerator

Village/town level is the finest AUTHORITATIVE geography in India and is the only level at which district splits are exactly resolvable, because new districts are constituted from whole tehsils and whole villages
evidence: Not fetched. The Census 2011 total of 1,210,854,977 and the 640-district count are marked verified in dossier sections 3.1 and 4.1 on the strength of the Wikipedia 'Census of India' article read on 2026-09-19; the PCA product itself was not opened, and the 2001->2011 district growth rates quoted (Gurgaon ~+74%, Rangareddy ~+48%, Bengaluru Urban ~+47%, Surat ~+42%, Gautam Buddha Nagar ~+51% against a national ~+17.7%) are flagged 'verify against the PCA before publishing'.
how_to_obtain: censusindia.gov.in publishes the PCA as per-state XLSX and the district/sub-district/village tables as downloadable tables; DataMeet and SHRUG redistribute cleaned copies. Take both the 2011 and 2001 PCA so the 2001->2011 district growth rates used for within-state differentiation (dossier section 3.5 step 3) can be computed rather than quoted.
notes: Step 1 of the project's denominator method and the base of the frozen 'c2011' geography.

name: Census of India Administrative Atlas / administrative-unit change series (1991, 2001, 2011)
publisher: Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India (ORGI), Ministry of Home Affairs
caveats: The district counts the dossier quotes against it (466 in 1991, 593 in 2001, 640 in 2011) are model knowledge and are explicitly flagged for verification
Stops at 2011 — it says nothing about the 160 districts created since, which is exactly the period we most need
Typically a scanned/typeset PDF atlas; expect hand-keying rather than parsing
evidence: Nothing fetched and nothing cited. Dossier section 4.1 names it only as the document against which the 1991/2001/2011 district counts should be checked.

name: Census of India 2027 — enumeration programme and (forthcoming) population products
publisher: Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India (ORGI), Ministry of Home Affairs
time_latest: population enumeration 9-28 Feb 2027; district tables expected ~2028
lag: 12-18 months from enumeration to district tables (expected)
caveats: Census 2021 was NEVER HELD — postponed in 2020 for COVID-19 and then deferred repeatedly. There is no 2021 count and there never will be

House-listing ran 1 Apr 2026 - Sep 2026; population enumeration 9-28 Feb 2027 with reference date 1 Mar 2027; snow-bound Himalayan areas enumerated Aug-Sep 2026 with reference date 1 Oct 2026 — two different reference dates in one census
Caste enumeration included for the first time since 1931

Realistic timetable for us: provisional totals mid-to-late 2027, Primary Census Abstract with district figures 2028, ward/village tables 2028-2029. PLAN FOR NO NEW OFFICIAL DISTRICT POPULATION BEFORE 2028
Will be enumerated on the current (~800-district) geography, so it will NOT retrospectively fix the 2011-frozen panel; it starts a third geography vintage
evidence: The programme and its dates are marked verified in dossier section 3.1 via the Wikipedia 'Census of India' article read on 2026-09-19. No census product exists to fetch yet.

Nothing to ingest before ~2027; the action item is a diarised re-base of the whole population panel when district tables land (dossier section 3.5 step 7), keeping the old denominator_version queryable so published figures stay reproducible.

name: Electoral roll elector counts by Assembly Constituency and district (annual Special Summary Revision)
publisher: Election Commission of India and the State Chief Electoral Officers
time_start: unknown (rolls have been published for decades; usable machine-readable series roughly 2000s onward)
time_latest: most recent annual Special Summary Revision
lag: weeks to months after the qualifying date
caveats: Electors are adults 18+ registered to vote, not population — the elector-to-population ratio is only stable ENOUGH within a state to flag districts where our projection is badly wrong, not to substitute for a census
AC boundaries are not district boundaries; ACs must be apportioned to districts, and delimitation (frozen since 2008, due to be revisited) will eventually break the AC panel too
Migration, duplicate and deceased entries, and roll-revision drives all move the count for non-demographic reasons
Published per-constituency as PDFs on 36 different CEO sites — the aggregation work is real
evidence: Nothing fetched. Dossier section 3.5 step 4 asserts from model knowledge that ECI publishes elector counts per AC and per district and revises them annually, and calls it 'the only annually-refreshed, official, sub-state population signal India has'.
how_to_obtain: eci.gov.in publishes Special Summary Revision statistics; each State CEO site (ceo.<state>.gov.in) publishes the per-AC electoral statistics and final roll PDFs. Harvest the AC-level elector totals per revision year, apportion to districts via the AC-to-district mapping, and use as an annual cross-check on the projected district panel — not as the denominator itself. Secondary proxies named in the dossier: PMJAY/Ayushman enrolment, Aadhaar saturation, NFHS-5 sampling frames, SECC 2011.
notes: Step 4 of the project's denominator method. The only annual sub-state population signal that exists; nothing else in this repository covers it as a denominator.

name: Local Government Directory (LGD) — district/sub-district/village codes with effective dates and change history
publisher: Ministry of Panchayati Raj / NIC, Government of India

caveats: The only government-wide district identifier with codes, effective dates and a change history, and what MoSPI/NIC systems use — but it describes only the CURRENT administrative set, so it cannot carry a time series on its own

For this domain's purposes, what is needed is a dated SNAPSHOT of the district table plus the change log, taken once per release and stored with a vintage tag, not a live lookup.

name: SHRUG — village/town spatial keys linking the 1991, 2001 and 2011 censuses, plus a district crosswalk
publisher: Development Data Lab (DDL)
time_latest: unknown (verify the current release and licence in Phase 2)
caveats: Stops at 2011. It solves the 1991-2011 half of the problem — the half we cannot do ourselves — but says nothing about the 160 districts created after 2011, which must be added forward from state gazette notifications
Academic product, not an official one: an authoritative-looking crosswalk that the government does not stand behind
The dossier session could not reach the site, so release version, file inventory and licence are all unconfirmed
evidence: Not fetched: the SHRUG site is egress-blocked in the dossier session. Dossier section 4.4 names it as the backbone of the geo_xwalk strategy — 'it publishes village/town-level keys linking the 1991, 2001 and 2011 censuses plus a district-level crosswalk, which is exactly the hard part already done'.
how_to_obtain: See 'geo-shrug' in research/sources/geospatial-boundaries.jsonl and 'civil-society-academic-ddl-shrug' in research/sources/civil-society-academic.jsonl — both carry a fetched download URL. Take the village-level keys and the district crosswalk, and check the licence terms before redistributing any derived boundary.
notes: Catalogued here as a METHODOLOGY artefact: it is the input to geo_xwalk(from_geo_key, from_vintage, to_geo_key, to_vintage, share, basis, source, confidence), which is what makes any pre-2011 time series joinable at all.

name: State gazette notifications constituting, merging and renaming districts (2011 onward)
publisher: State governments (revenue departments) and State Government Presses
geo_coverage: all States/UTs (in practice: Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal and ~20 others)
time_latest: ongoing (most recent major events: Rajasthan 2024-12-28, Assam 2023-01-01)
caveats: This is the ONLY authoritative record of which tehsils and villages moved from which parent district to which child, and therefore the only exact basis for the apportionment weight in geo_xwalk

640 (Census 2011) -> 800 districts (Dec 2025) = +160 (+25%); Telangana 10 -> 31 (one day, 2016-10-11) -> 33; Andhra Pradesh 13 -> 26 in one day (2022-04-04); Rajasthan 33 -> 50 (Aug 2023) -> 41 (2024-12-28, 17 of 19 new districts SCRAPPED); Assam merged four districts back on 2023-01-01
MERGES and REVERSALS break the near-universal engineering assumption that districts only split. A split can be apportioned; a merge destroys the distinction permanently going forward

Renames are silent killers on a name join: Gurgaon->Gurugram (2016), Allahabad->Prayagraj (2018), Faizabad->Ayodhya (2018), Aurangabad->Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Osmanabad->Dharashiv (2023), Hoshangabad->Narmadapuram (2021), plus the Karnataka set (Bangalore->Bengaluru, Mysore->Mysuru, Belgaum->Belagavi, Gulbarga->Kalaburagi, Bellary->Ballari, Bijapur->Vijayapura, Tumkur->Tumakuru, Shimoga->Shivamogga)
Published on 36 different state press sites in 22 languages, usually as scanned PDFs, often without a stable index. Some states will need an RTI
Police geography moves independently of revenue geography — UP's revenue districts have been stable at 75 since ~2012 while its POLICE map was recut by commissionerate creation in 2020, 2021 and 2022
evidence: Nothing fetched. Dossier section 4.4 asserts from model knowledge that new districts are constituted from whole tehsils and whole villages by state gazette notification, and prescribes extending SHRUG forward using those notifications; section 4.2 lists the individual reorganisation events and dates.
how_to_obtain: Per state: the State Government Press / e-gazette portal (e.g. egazette.<state>.gov.in) and the revenue department's notifications page. Where no online gazette archive exists, file an RTI with the state revenue department asking for the notification constituting district X and the list of tehsils/villages transferred. Prioritise the states in the caveats — Telangana, AP, Rajasthan, Assam, Arunachal, MP, WB — which between them account for most of the +160.
notes: The forward half of the crosswalk problem: SHRUG gives us 1991-2011, these notifications give us 2011-now. No other dossier in this repository covers them.

name: Wikipedia — List of districts in India / Districts of India (English)
publisher: Wikimedia Foundation / Wikipedia contributors
lag: days to weeks after a state notification
caveats: The 800 count includes Mahe and Yanam as census districts and a TEMPORARY Maha Kumbh Mela district, and excludes Itanagar Capital Complex — the definition of 'district' in the count is not the same as LGD's
Per-state sub-lists disagree with the dossier's own figures in places (Andhra Pradesh shows 28 against a documented 26; West Bengal shows 27) and are flagged for verification
Tier-5 crowd-sourced source, but in practice the FASTEST-updating district register that exists — faster than LGD in the days after a notification
evidence: Read 2026-09-19. Supplied the headline finding of dossier section 4.1: 800 districts as of 9 December 2025, against 640 at Census 2011 — +160 (+25%) — plus the Telangana sequence (10 at formation 2014-06-02, 31 on 2016-10-11, 33 on 2019-02-17) and the J&K/Ladakh reorganisation arithmetic, both marked VERIFIED in section 4.2.
how_to_obtain: Open the article or fetch via the MediaWiki API; pin the revision id.
notes: URL reconstructed from the article title recorded in the dossier; the dossier itself records no URLs. Wikipedia is tier-5 evidence: use it to find the primary document, never as the citation in the product. Useful as a change DETECTOR — diff it monthly to catch a new district before LGD publishes the code — never as the register itself.

landing.title: List of districts in India - Wikipedia

name: Wikipedia — Law enforcement in India (English)
publisher: Wikimedia Foundation / Wikipedia contributors
caveats: Gives a COUNT of commissionerates, not a list with dates, and certainly not polygons — India publishes no national polygon layer for police jurisdictions at any level
Tier-5 crowd-sourced source
evidence: Read 2026-09-19. States that 68 cities and suburban areas currently operate under the commissionerate system — the figure used in dossier section 5.4 to size the police-geography problem.
how_to_obtain: Open the article or fetch via the MediaWiki API; pin the revision id.
notes: URL reconstructed from the article title recorded in the dossier; the dossier itself records no URLs. Wikipedia is tier-5 evidence: use it to find the primary document, never as the citation in the product. Relevant because NCRB's reporting units are police units: one revenue district can become two or three NCRB rows (Pune City + Pimpri-Chinchwad + Pune Rural), and a name join drops the ones that match no revenue district.

name: Wikipedia — Rape in India (English)
publisher: Wikimedia Foundation / Wikipedia contributors
caveats: A secondary summary of NFHS-derived analyses, an NCRB report and press coverage — every figure must be traced to its primary source before it appears in the product
The three headline figures it carries (>90%, 71%, ~99%) are not the same estimand and are not comparable to each other
Tier-5 crowd-sourced source on a subject where a wrong number is actively harmful
evidence: Read 2026-09-19. Supplied the under-reporting evidence table in dossier section 6.1: independent analyses of NFHS data indicating >90% of sexual assaults go unreported; NCRB's own 2006 report putting unreported rape at 71%; the Livemint (25 Oct 2015) '99% cases of sexual assaults go unreported' figure; and a UN Women global benchmark of ~11% of rape/sexual assault ever reported.
how_to_obtain: Open the article or fetch via the MediaWiki API; pin the revision id, and follow its citations to the primary documents before using any number.
notes: URL reconstructed from the article title recorded in the dossier; the dossier itself records no URLs. Wikipedia is tier-5 evidence: use it to find the primary document, never as the citation in the product. This is the single best-evidenced statement in the dossier that a map of reported crime is partly a map of police responsiveness.

name: NCRB report (2006) — estimate that 71% of rapes went unreported
publisher: National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Ministry of Home Affairs
caveats: 20 years old and pre-dates the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013, which changed the definition of rape — the 71% is not directly comparable to any post-2013 figure
Known only second-hand: the dossier has it from the Wikipedia 'Rape in India' article, not from the NCRB document
Precise title, volume and table are unknown — it may be a chapter in a Crime in India volume rather than a standalone report
Remarkable chiefly because it is NCRB acknowledging its own undercount; NCRB publishes no equivalent estimate for the principal offence rule
evidence: Not fetched: ncrb.gov.in is egress-blocked. Cited in dossier section 6.1 as 'NCRB's own 2006 report (cited in the same article)', the article being the Wikipedia 'Rape in India' page read on 2026-09-19.
how_to_obtain: Follow the citation in the Wikipedia 'Rape in India' article to the exact NCRB document, then retrieve it from ncrb.gov.in's archive (or the Internet Archive) from an unproxied network. If it cannot be located, file an RTI with NCRB for the 2006 publication containing the unreported-rape estimate and its methodology — the methodology is worth more to us than the number.
notes: The only official Indian undercount estimate the dossier could find for any crime category.

name: '99% cases of sexual assaults go unreported, govt data shows' (Livemint, 25 October 2015)
publisher: Livemint / HT Media
caveats: A journalistic comparison of NFHS self-reported victimisation against NCRB registered cases — two instruments with different definitions, reference periods and populations. TREAT ~99% AS AN UPPER BOUND, not an estimate
Media-derived; the dossier explicitly downgrades it relative to the NFHS and NCRB figures
Known second-hand via the Wikipedia 'Rape in India' article; the piece itself was not opened
evidence: Not fetched. Cited in the dossier section 6.1 evidence table with exact publication, date and headline, sourced from the Wikipedia 'Rape in India' article read on 2026-09-19.
how_to_obtain: Search livemint.com for the headline, or the Internet Archive for October 2015. What we actually want is its method — which NFHS table and which CII table it divided — so the calculation can be reproduced and bounded properly.
notes: Catalogued so the ~99% figure has a provenance record: it is the number a journalist will quote back at us, and we should be able to say exactly what it is and is not.

name: National Family Health Survey 5 (2019-21) — spousal violence and help-seeking module (national report Ch. 15)
publisher: International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS) for the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare
geo_coverage: all-India, all States/UTs and all districts
caveats: The dossier's figures here are MODEL KNOWLEDGE and are explicitly flagged for verification against the NFHS-5 national report Ch.15: ~29-30% of ever-married women 18-49 report spousal physical/sexual violence, only ~14% of those ever sought help, and only ~1.5% sought help from the police — implying >98% never reaches the police
Prevalence among ever-married women 18-49, not incidence, not all women, and not all violence — it is not a crime count and must never be subtracted from or added to an FIR count
Marital rape is a STRUCTURAL zero in the crime data: sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife aged 18+ is excepted from BNS 63, so it is legally unreportable, not merely under-reported
District estimates come from a sampling design with district-level precision limits; small-district estimates carry wide intervals
evidence: Nothing fetched. Dossier section 6.1 marks this row '(Model knowledge — verify against the NFHS-5 national report, Ch. 15)'.
how_to_obtain: Download the NFHS-5 India report and the state/district factsheets from rchiips.org/nfhs or main.mohfw.gov.in; the microdata is available from the DHS Program on registration. See research/sources/civil-society-academic.jsonl for the fuller NFHS entries.
notes: Catalogued here for one specific product purpose (dossier section 6.4 measure 5): spousal violence is the ONE category where district-level reported and experienced figures can be shown side by side and the difference labelled 'the reporting gap'. Doing it for one category teaches users to read the rest of the map correctly.

name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, (2014) 2 SCC 1 (Constitution Bench, 12 November 2013)
publisher: Supreme Court of India
caveats: Held FIR registration mandatory under CrPC s.154 where the information discloses a cognizable offence, with preliminary inquiry permitted only in specified categories (matrimonial/family, commercial, medical negligence, corruption, abnormal delay) and capped at 7 days

BNSS s.173(3) re-introduced a DISCRETIONARY preliminary inquiry of up to 14 days for cognizable offences punishable with 3-7 years — a partial statutory rollback. Registered crime falling in 2024-25 may be a statutory artefact, not an improvement
A legal duty is not a behaviour: burking continued after 2013. The judgment is the benchmark against which non-registration is measured, not evidence that it stopped
evidence: Not fetched. Dossier section 6.2 gives the full citation, the bench, the date and the holding, including the list of permitted preliminary-inquiry categories and the 7-day cap.
how_to_obtain: Retrieve from main.sci.gov.in (judgment search), the eSCR portal, or Indian Kanoon. Needed as the legal baseline in the methodology page, and to date the pre/post-2013 registration regime in the series_break documentation.
notes: Pairs with BNSS s.173(3): the two together define why 2013 and 2024 are both registration-regime breaks, in opposite directions.

name: Status of Policing in India Report (SPIR) series — 2018, 2019, 2023, 2025
publisher: Common Cause and Lokniti - Centre for the Study of Developing Societies (CSDS)
geo_coverage: multi-state samples of citizens and serving police personnel (not all-India coverage)
caveats: Survey evidence of attitudes and self-reported behaviour on non-registration, not a measurement of how many FIRs were refused
Sample states differ between editions, so the series is not a panel
Egress-blocked in the dossier session; edition list, contents and licence unconfirmed
evidence: Not fetched: '(All egress-blocked here; verify in Phase 2.)' Dossier section 6.2 names the series, both publishing bodies and the four editions (2018, 2019, 2023, 2025), and describes it as surveying citizens and police on exactly the non-registration question.
how_to_obtain: Download from commoncause.in and lokniti.org from an unproxied network; the reports are free PDFs. Extract the non-registration and trust items, per state, per edition. See research/sources/civil-society-academic.jsonl for the fuller entry.
notes: Supplies the attitudinal half of the burking evidence; the statistical half is the registration_propensity detector in dossier section 6.2.

name: Second Administrative Reforms Commission, 5th Report — 'Public Order' (2007)
publisher: Second Administrative Reforms Commission, Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, Government of India
caveats: 19 years old; its statistics are of historical interest only
Its value to us is INSTITUTIONAL ACKNOWLEDGEMENT — an official body identifying non-registration as systemic — which is what makes the caveat quotable rather than merely asserted
Egress-blocked in the dossier session
evidence: Not fetched: '(All egress-blocked here; verify in Phase 2.)' Dossier section 6.2 names the commission, the report number and title, the year, and the finding relied on.
how_to_obtain: Download from darpg.gov.in (Second ARC reports archive) from an unproxied network. We need only the paragraphs on crime registration and burking, for the methodology page's citation list.
notes: Pairs with the Padmanabhaiah Committee (2000) as the two official acknowledgements the product can cite when it says a low number is not a green light.

name: Report of the Committee on Police Reforms (Padmanabhaiah Committee), 2000
publisher: Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
caveats: 26 years old; cited for its identification of non-registration as systemic, not for any current figure
May only exist as a scanned PDF, or via third-party mirrors (Bureau of Police Research & Development, police-reform NGOs) rather than an MHA page
Egress-blocked in the dossier session
evidence: Not fetched: '(All egress-blocked here; verify in Phase 2.)' Dossier section 6.2 names the committee and year and the finding relied on.
how_to_obtain: Try mha.gov.in and bprd.nic.in from an unproxied network; failing that, the Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative (humanrightsinitiative.org) and other police-reform NGOs mirror the historic police-reform committee reports. Only the chapter on crime registration is needed.
